_readme: AARC exemplar set v10.1. Passage: research/exemplar_passage_spacing.md (original text, CC BY 4.0, exemplar use only, never a formal evaluation passage). Items drafted by Claude (AI) on 15 Oct 2026 for the researcher's review. permission_confirmed is false until the researcher has reviewed each item; then set it to true and import in Model settings > Exemplar library. Process labels follow the PIRLS 2026 framework (Sabatini et al., 2024, pp. 12-15); adult informational tasks are informed by PISA 2018 (OECD, 2019, pp. 34-36).

exemplars.passage_excerpt: an adult article on the spacing effect: spreading study over time versus cramming
exemplars.stem: What did Ebbinghaus memorise in his experiments?
options: Obscure facts
Foreign vocabulary
Lists of nonsense syllables
Simple mathematics procedures
evidence: he memorised lists of nonsense syllables
exemplars.process_rationale: The answer is stated in one sentence and the stem and correct option use the text's own words (PIRLS 2026 p. 12: exact words within a sentence or two = focus on and retrieve; PISA 2018 p. 34: literal or close to literal matching).
exemplars.distractor_notes: All three distractors are materials the text DOES mention, for other studies (obscure facts: the online study; foreign vocabulary and mathematics procedures: later research), so the reader must locate the right sentence rather than recognise a familiar phrase.

exemplars.skill: infer a consequence from a stated finding
exemplars.passage_excerpt: an adult article on the spacing effect: spreading study over time versus cramming
exemplars.stem: Based on the online study, what is most likely true of a person who must remember some facts for a year but reviews them one day after learning them?
options: Their gap is shorter than ideal
Their gap is the ideal one for long-term memory
Their review is wasted, because a single review has no effect
They are certain to forget everything within a week
evidence: people tested after a year benefited most from a gap of several weeks
exemplars.process_rationale: The text never says that a one-day gap is too short for a year. The reader must connect the stated finding (several weeks is best for a year) to the new case. The inference rests on one place in the text and the meaning stays clear (PIRLS 2026 p. 13). It is not a paraphrase of a stated sentence: the answer itself is nowhere in the text.
exemplars.distractor_notes: B reverses the finding; C is unsupported (the study shows that reviews help); D over-generalises from 'shorter than ideal' to total forgetting.

exemplars.skill: integrate a causal explanation across paragraphs
exemplars.passage_excerpt: an adult article on the spacing effect: spreading study over time versus cramming
exemplars.stem: Taking paragraphs 4 and 5 together, why can a study method that feels easy be a poor guide to lasting learning?
options: Easy methods work only for complex skills such as writing an argument
Feeling at ease means the learner has stopped paying attention
Rereading takes more total time than spacing the same material
Material reread straight away has not been forgotten, so there is no effortful recall to strengthen it
evidence: learners tend to mistake this ease for learning
this effort of recalling it is what strengthens the memory
exemplars.link: Paragraph 4 says immediate rereading feels easy; paragraph 5 says the effort of recalling partly forgotten material strengthens memory. Together: the ease exists precisely because the effortful recall that builds memory is missing.
exemplars.process_rationale: No sentence states this causal chain. The reader must synthesise an explanation from two paragraphs: a concept (the ease and the missing effort are two sides of one process) that is grounded in the text but not written in it (PIRLS 2026 p. 14; PISA 2018 p. 35: causal coherence relationships across the passage). The answer reuses words from the text ('effortful recall'), which is allowed: what matters is that the relationship has to be built by the reader.
exemplars.distractor_notes: A misapplies a detail from the limitations paragraph; B is a plausible personal theory the text never offers; C contradicts the text's premise that total study time stays the same.

exemplars.passage_excerpt: an adult article on the spacing effect: spreading study over time versus cramming
exemplars.stem: Which two facts are both stated in the passage?
options: Ebbinghaus tested only himself, and the online study tested people up to a year later
Ebbinghaus tested only himself, and the online study tested people up to a week later
Ebbinghaus tested many students, and the online study tested people up to a year later
Ebbinghaus tested many students, and the online study tested people up to a week later
evidence: Using himself as the only participant
were then tested up to a year later
exemplars.why_bad: This is NOT process 3. It staples together two unrelated facts from different paragraphs and asks the reader to retrieve each one; the options are a 2 x 2 grid of 'X and Y' combinations. No interpretation or synthesis is needed, and finding the two evidence spans in different paragraphs does not make it integration.

exemplars.skill: judge how well a claim is supported
exemplars.passage_excerpt: an adult article on the spacing effect: spreading study over time versus cramming
exemplars.stem: Which statement best judges how well the author supports the claim that schools should build review into their timetables?
options: Completely, because one study with more than a thousand adults proves that spacing works in schools
Reasonably well, because the research evidence is broad, and the author openly admits it still needs testing in real classrooms
Not at all, because Ebbinghaus was the only participant in his experiments
Poorly, because the author never discusses any weaknesses in the evidence
evidence: What researchers still need are careful studies in real classrooms
exemplars.process_rationale: The reader steps back from the content to judge the quality of the author's argument, weighing the strength of the evidence against the limitations the author states: a justified judgment about the text (PIRLS 2026 p. 15; PISA 2018 p. 35: assessing quality and credibility). Each option is a judgment plus a reason, and only one reason is supported by the text.
exemplars.distractor_notes: A over-states one study (obscure facts, online, not schools); C ignores the century of later evidence; D is contradicted by the paragraph on limits.
